overview: The atlas calls this layer “Japan (USA),” but Japan did not become part of the United States. The name compresses the U.S.-led Allied occupation, which began after surrender in 1945 and ended when the peace treaty took effect in 1952. Japan remained a country whose government operated under the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers. After 1952 it was sovereign while linked to the United States through bases and security agreements. The atlas keeps this id until its 1960 snapshot. Its four-part polygon covers Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu and islands represented by coarse coastlines; it omits Okinawa, Amami and Ogasawara. This geometry is not a jurisdictional inventory: several coastal city-center probes also fall outside its shorelines. The time span fuses two phases that require separate reading. Occupation authority shaped government and reconstruction through 1952; afterward, sovereign Japan negotiated its American security relationship. The 1960 endpoint marks an atlas switch back to japan-1914, not collapse, annexation, independence or succession. This card separates map label, state, occupation chain of command, base presence, and daily life, and never invents a “Japan-USA” polity.

periods.title: 1945 to 1946: surrender, occupation, hunger, and return
periods.summary: Japan formally surrendered in September 1945. Cities and transport networks were damaged, rations were inadequate, black markets mattered, and people returned from a collapsed empire. Occupation authority constrained the government while demobilization, relief, accountability, and the first democratic reforms began.

periods.title: 1946 to 1947: votes, rights, and a new constitution
periods.summary: Women voted in a general election for the first time in April 1946. Japanese and occupation participants contested constitutional drafts. The resulting text was promulgated in November, grounding government in popular sovereignty and stating equality, social rights, pacifism, and a new legal basis for marriage.

periods.title: 1947 to 1948: constitution and school system take effect
periods.summary: The Constitution took effect on May 3, 1947. The School Education Law created a six-three-three-four structure, with nine years of compulsory schooling. New tentative courses of study introduced social studies and other subjects, while shortages of rooms, books, teachers, food, and clothing shaped classrooms.

periods.title: 1948 to 1949: stabilization and the reverse course
periods.summary: Occupation priorities moved toward economic stabilization and anticommunism. The Dodge program tightened finance and fixed the exchange rate at 360 yen per dollar. Recovery policy reduced inflation but imposed painful adjustments, while occupation censorship of mail, print, broadcasts, film, and telephone communications persisted into 1949.

periods.title: 1949 to 1950: fiscal restraint and public-health rebuilding
periods.summary: Fiscal stabilization and industrial restructuring continued as Cold War priorities hardened. Official histories record those policy shifts, while reorganized health centers pursued infectious-disease control, sanitation, and maternal and child care. These sources show institutional priorities, not proof that every reform reached households or localities equally.

periods.title: 1950 to 1951: Korean War demand accelerates recovery
periods.summary: The Korean War transformed the regional setting and brought large procurement demand to Japanese producers. Output, shipping, repair, and related services revived more quickly as Japan’s strategic role deepened. Fiscal histories establish that turn, but they do not prove that wages, living standards, or access improved evenly.

periods.title: 1951 to 1952: peace treaty and occupation endpoint
periods.summary: Japan signed the San Francisco Peace Treaty in September 1951. It entered into force on April 28, 1952, ending the Allied occupation of the main islands. The treaty left specified island groups under separate U.S. administration, while a security relationship allowed a continuing American military presence.

periods.title: 1952 to 1953: one atlas interval crosses a legal divide
periods.summary: The main islands were sovereign after April 1952, although the japan-usa polygon persists until the 1960 snapshot. Okinawa remained outside this feature under U.S. authority, with the Government of the Ryukyu Islands established in 1952. One atlas label therefore spans different legal and administrative conditions.

periods.title: 1953 to 1955: reconstruction becomes visible growth
periods.summary: Population and production recovered, cities drew migrants, and consumer goods became more visible, though scarcity and inequality remained. Museum evidence links black-market reconstruction to electrification and heavy industry. National totals require care because territorial coverage and the status of Okinawa and Amami changed across statistics.

periods.title: 1955 to 1960: high growth, pollution, culture, and Anpo
periods.summary: Rapid growth expanded factories, transport, suburbs, media, and household consumption. Minamata disease was officially reported in 1956, exposing grave industrial harm. Artists tested new media, while mass opposition surrounded the revised 1960 security treaty. The atlas changed labels at 1960, not because Japan collapsed.

sections.title: Read the atlas label, government, islands, and writing carefully

items.text: The exact live id is japan-usa, labeled “Japan (USA)” for 1945 to 1960. It has one observed border feature and a missing deep card. Its imported summary describes modern Japan generally, so it cannot explain occupation government, the exact geometry, or this deliberately bounded postwar interval.

The 1945 feature is one MultiPolygon with four components, four rings, 324 positions, and a bounding box from about 129.34 to 145.45 degrees east and 30.89 to 45.43 degrees north. It has no direct shared arcs. Long-range snapshots confirm that this hybrid id exists only here, between japan-1914 regimes.

The surrender instrument placed the authority of the emperor and Japanese government under the Supreme Commander, while the peace treaty took effect in 1952. Together these documents define occupation and its legal endpoint; neither records annexation to the United States, a changed citizenship, or a sovereign “Japan-USA” polity.

Okinawa, Amami, and Ogasawara lie outside the exact polygon. Okinawan archives document U.S. institutions continuing after 1952 and a different administrative path. These island histories belong as explicit comparisons, not evidence that occupation of the four main islands lasted fifteen years or that all excluded islands shared one timetable.

Contemporaneous written sample, from Constitution Article 24: 「婚姻は、両性の合意のみに基いて成立し」 (Kon'in wa, ryōsei no gōi no mi ni motozuite seiritsu shi), “Marriage shall be based only on the mutual consent of both sexes.” This securely dated formal Japanese legal text is not a sample of every person’s speech.

sections.title: Homes, food, clothing, transport, and neighborhood life

items.text: Air raids left severe housing shortages in many cities. Families doubled up, adapted damaged buildings, built makeshift rooms, or searched regulated rental markets while timber, land, and capital remained constrained. Reconstruction varied by city and tenure, so photographs of barracks or new estates cannot define every household.

Ration cards did not guarantee enough food. People queued, substituted unfamiliar ingredients, traded possessions, cultivated small plots, and used black markets at legal and personal risk. The National Showa Memorial Museum preserves objects and images of these shortages; a major synthesis connects them to defeat without making Tokyo universal.

Rural livelihood-improvement groups, often organized around women, identified household problems and tested changes with limited local resources. Documented projects included improved kamado stoves, nutrition, and sanitation. They show practical local experimentation and women’s organizing, not instant nationwide modernization or proof that every participating household changed alike.

Clothes and bedding were valuable household resources. Families patched garments, remade adult clothing for children, shared bedding, and conserved fuel before later consumer recovery widened choices. Museum displays can make such practices tangible, but their reconstructed rooms represent selected experiences rather than one standard postwar Japanese home.

By 1958 to 1960, a studied Tokyo suburban white-collar community organized days around commuting, school, neighborhood obligations, shopping, and a wage-earner household ideal. That close fieldwork illuminates emerging middle-class rhythms while remaining one pseudonymous suburb, not a template for farmers, miners, Ainu villages, or crowded lodgers.

sections.title: Work, farms, factories, labor, and economic recovery

items.text: Millions returned from former imperial territories, but “repatriate” covered unequal routes from Manchuria, Korea, Taiwan, Sakhalin, the Pacific, and elsewhere. Returnees searched for relatives, housing, ration registration, schooling, and work while bringing different losses and skills. Reintegration helped redefine who counted within postwar Japan.

The Constitution protected workers’ rights to organize, bargain, and act collectively, yet legal language did not settle workplace power. The drafting record establishes a negotiated guarantee, not actual wages, hazards, job security, union strength, or voice in factories, mines, offices, farms, and casual employment.

Land reform transferred much tenanted farmland to cultivators and altered village power, while everyday gains still depended on yields, prices, credit, family labor, and local administration. Rural livelihood programs added household, nutrition, and sanitation projects. Neither reform erased small plots, gendered work, or regional inequality.

Economic stabilization checked inflation through tight budgets, credit restraint, and a fixed 360-yen exchange rate. Those policies improved planning conditions but also forced closures, layoffs, and household adjustment. A macroeconomic turning point should be read beside rationing, housing, and labor evidence, since national recovery never arrived evenly.

Korean War procurement accelerated orders for Japanese factories, shipping, repair, and services. It helped convert fragile stabilization into faster recovery, but prosperity was neither automatic nor morally simple: a nearby war generated demand, and benefits differed by industry, firm, region, employment status, and household responsibilities.

sections.title: Families, women, marriage, migration, and belonging

items.text: Article 24 grounded marriage in mutual consent and equal spousal rights, challenging the prewar household system in law. Revised family rules changed marriage, divorce, inheritance, and household authority, but constitutional equality did not remove unpaid labor, employment barriers, domestic conflict, or the pressure to perform respectable family roles.

The election law was revised in December 1945, and women cast ballots in the April 1946 general election. Enfranchisement opened formal political participation and brought women into the Diet, yet it did not guarantee equal power within parties, workplaces, homes, unions, or local institutions.

Births surged after the war, then birth rates fell through the 1950s as mortality also changed. Official vital statistics let readers trace births, deaths, natural increase, and infant mortality, but national aggregates conceal sharp differences by income, city and countryside, region, pollution exposure, and access to care.

Zainichi Korean families faced a post-imperial shift from colonial-subject status toward foreign registration and legal insecurity. A politically contested program to North Korea began in 1959. It should not be reduced to simple homecoming: family division, information, discrimination, politics, and individual motives differed.

Late-1950s salaryman households became a powerful ideal, with paid work centered on the husband and home management associated with the wife. Fieldwork in one Tokyo suburb shows aspirations, budgeting, schooling, and neighborhood ties, while its narrow setting warns against calling this the timeless or universal Japanese family.

sections.title: Children, play, care, meals, and unequal childhoods

items.text: Children experienced bereavement, missing relatives, damaged homes, hunger, street work, institutional care, and abrupt adult responsibilities. Others retained family support and returned to school quickly. Museum sections devoted to children preserve photographs, school objects, toys, and ration-era materials without turning one display into a universal childhood.

The postwar baby boom enlarged young cohorts while infant mortality fell substantially across the following years. Those trends reflect food, infection control, maternal care, household conditions, and wider recovery, but a national series cannot show each child’s survival chances or isolate one program as the cause.

School lunches resumed as emergency nutrition and gradually expanded, making eating part of the school day as well as household life. Menus and coverage varied, so not every pupil received the same meal. Lunch programs connected imported supplies, local kitchens, health checks, attendance, and lessons about nutrition.

Play survived scarcity through handmade balls, stilts, paper games, songs, improvised toys, and neighborhood space, while organized sport also returned. The postwar National Athletic Meet began in 1946. Objects and government histories reveal possibilities, but children’s leisure depended on work duties, safety, disability, gender, and local resources.

Ainu children in Hokkaido inherited living languages, stories, foodways, games, craft, and kin ties while facing assimilation and discrimination. Postwar cultural preservation could support transmission yet also reshape practice for schools, tourism, or display. Evidence must remain community-specific rather than presenting one frozen Ainu tradition.

The 1947 School Education Law established six years of elementary school, three of lower secondary, three of upper secondary, and four of university, with nine compulsory years. The structure widened a common route on paper, while buildings, fees beyond compulsory school, entrance competition, disability access, and family resources shaped attendance.

Tentative 1947 courses of study replaced militarized schooling with new subjects and methods, including social studies, homemaking, and freer study periods. Teachers had to interpret changing guidance with uneven textbooks, materials, training, and classroom space. A national curriculum therefore describes an intention, not identical lessons everywhere.

Education reform expanded local boards, coeducation, new textbooks, and democratic language while occupation review influenced acceptable content. Japanese officials, educators, parents, students, and occupation staff all participated with unequal power. Later policy also emphasized science and technical training as reconstruction moved toward industrial growth.

Bomb damage, teacher shortages, overcrowding, and lack of books made reform materially difficult. Communities reused rooms, ran shifts, shared supplies, and rebuilt while pupils also needed food and clothing. Institutional expansion was real, but judging it only by laws or enrollment hides what teaching required each day.

Constitution Article 26 recognized an equal right to education and required guardians to ensure compulsory education without tuition. Legal equality mattered, yet progression beyond compulsory school still reflected household income, location, gender expectations, examination systems, health, and the uneven availability of upper-secondary and university places.

sections.title: Medicine, nutrition, disease, disability, and care

items.text: Postwar public-health administration rebuilt health centers and prioritized tuberculosis, enteric and other infectious diseases, maternal and child care, sanitation, and health education. Clinics, hospitals, pharmacies, midwives, doctors, nurses, and household caregivers formed an uneven system; institutional design cannot prove equal treatment in every prefecture.

A nationwide nutrition survey began amid 1945 scarcity, measuring diet and physical condition to guide relief and policy. Such surveys made malnutrition visible in standardized categories, yet sampling and measurement cannot reproduce every meal, black-market purchase, rural harvest, institutional ration, or unequal household distribution.

Rural health improved through interacting changes in food, maternal and child services, tuberculosis control, agriculture, household environments, social education, and local organization. The evidence supports a multicausal story, not a single medical miracle. Mountain villages, fishing communities, and peri-urban settlements followed different routes.

Occupation censorship restricted public circulation of some Hiroshima and Nagasaki images until 1952. Later survivor drawings and testimony became vital evidence of remembered destruction. Their creation dates and retrospective character must remain visible; this visual-history source documents representation and censorship, not a complete medical history of atomic-bomb survivors.

Minamata disease was officially reported in 1956 after residents developed severe neurological illness linked to contaminated seafood and industrial mercury. Recognition and effective response lagged behind suffering. The case exposes how rapid growth could transfer corporate and regulatory costs onto fishing families, children, disabled people, and polluted ecosystems.

sections.title: Water, toilets, waste, insects, and environmental sanitation

items.text: Toilets ranged from older privies to improved designs, and campaigns connected excreta management with parasites and disease. Reform did not produce one national fixture: building type, water access, municipal service, farm use of night soil, cost, and local enforcement shaped what households actually used.

Neighborhood movements against mosquitoes and flies targeted standing water, exposed waste, drains, breeding sites, and household practices. Their history shows sanitation as repeated collective labor, not only pipes or expert orders. Participation and results varied, so “eradication” language would overstate what local campaigns achieved.

Reorganized health centers joined infectious-disease surveillance, maternal and child care, sanitation, and health teaching within local administration. Services and access differed by region and population. The institutional history establishes responsibilities and priorities, not equal staffing, trust, transport, treatment, or results in every community.

Livelihood-improvement groups addressed smoke, stove efficiency, kitchen work, food preparation, drainage, and household cleanliness with locally available materials. These practical changes could reduce drudgery and health risks, yet programs relied heavily on women’s labor and could turn structural shortages into private household responsibility.

Industrial recovery intensified water pollution before regulation caught up. The 1958 water-quality laws covered limited waters and did not prevent disasters already unfolding, including Minamata. Sanitation history must therefore include both household waste control and the much larger effluent decisions of factories and government.

sections.title: Power, censorship, minorities, bases, and contested democracy

items.text: The surrender instrument subordinated Japanese governing authority to the Supreme Commander, while constitutional drafting records show negotiation over equality and social rights. Democratic reform therefore occurred under unequal occupation power and Japanese participation. These documents establish formal authority and debate, not identical implementation in every institution or locality.

Occupation censors monitored mail, telephones, newspapers, broadcasting, books, and film from 1945 into 1949. The survival of censor marks makes that control concrete. New freedoms and secret review coexisted, so a story of uncomplicated democratization would miss a central contradiction of the period.

Debate over Hiroshima and Nagasaki, imperial violence, war responsibility, the emperor, and victimhood unfolded under censorship and later Cold War priorities. Visual evidence resurfacing in 1952 altered public memory. Careful history distinguishes Japanese civilian suffering from crimes committed across Asia and the Pacific.

Hokkaido was and remains an Ainu homeland. The 1899 assimilation regime and discrimination continued to shape postwar language, land, work, schooling, and cultural transmission. Ainu people were citizens within the polygon, not a vanished preface to Japanese history, and communities made different choices about preservation and public performance.

Okinawans outside this polygon endured displacement, refugee camps, prolonged U.S. rule, and expanding bases. Archives document coercive land acquisition and island-wide protest. This separate history corrects the atlas label: American military power lasted beyond 1952, but its legal form and local burden were not identical across Japan.

sections.title: Culture, technology, achievements, surprises, and the 1960 seam

items.text: Sony introduced the TR-55 transistor radio in 1955 after pursuing transistor licensing and development. The exact model offers a concrete engineering milestone and a portable form of listening. A corporate history is reliable for product chronology, but it cannot prove immediate ownership or shared listening habits nationwide.

Refrigerators, washing machines, and vacuum cleaners became symbols of changing domestic life, though early models were expensive and diffusion was uneven. Mechanical heritage records preserve actual machines and dates. Their labor-saving promise also raises questions about who performed housework and who could afford electricity and space.

Toyota’s first-generation Crown appeared in 1955 as a tangible marker of domestic automobile engineering and industrial recovery. It did not mean that most families owned cars. Roads, public transport, company fleets, taxis, prices, and worker conditions belong beside the celebrated model in any account of mobility.

Fun fact: Chicken Ramen went on sale on August 25, 1958. The product made quick preparation and food-processing technology visible in an ordinary meal, but a company origin story cannot show instant universal adoption. Rice, noodles, fish, vegetables, regional dishes, ration memories, and household budgets still shaped diets.

From 1955, Tokyo artists combined photography, graphic design, performance, film, sound, and protest as commerce and politics accelerated. Their work makes cultural experimentation part of high growth, while remaining city-centered. At 1960 the atlas changes ids; Japanese people, institutions, arguments, and creativity continue across that seam.

ending.text: At the 1960 snapshot, the exact japan-usa id disappears and the atlas resumes japan-1914 over the same four main-island components. This is a label correction, not a fall, annexation, independence, or new country: the Allied occupation had already ended in 1952. The revised U.S.-Japan security treaty preserved American facilities, while Okinawa remained under separate U.S. administration outside this polygon. The Japanese state continues across the atlas seam. The packet therefore records continuity, leaves fell null, and creates no successor polity.
